case_brief.incident_description: Thabo worked for the employer for five years. He was accused of insubordination after refusing to drive a delivery vehicle that he said had faulty brakes. He asked for the instruction to be put in writing. He was told at 08:00 that a disciplinary hearing would take place at 10:00 the same day. He was not allowed to bring a colleague. His direct manager, who had issued the instruction, chaired the hearing. Thabo denied being insubordinate and said he was concerned about safety. He was dismissed immediately after the hearing.
case_brief.original_client_narrative: I refused to drive the truck because the brakes were faulty. My manager said I was insubordinate and then chaired my hearing two hours later. I was not allowed anyone with me and I was fired the same day.
legal_basis: Occupational Health and Safety Act context
case_brief.recommended_next_step: Without Prejudice settlement letter addressing procedural unfairness and the safety context.
weaknesses: Employer may argue refusal of instruction was misconduct

letter:
Background

1. We are instructed by our client, Mr Thabo Mokoena, in relation to the termination of his employment with Northstar Logistics (Pty) Ltd on 21 October 2026. This letter is written without prejudice and subject to contract, on the basis that nothing in it constitutes an admission of fact or liability by either party, and all of our client's rights are reserved to pursue the appropriate statutory remedy without further notice in the event that the matter is not resolved. Any response to this letter should be directed to our offices.

2. Our client reports that he was employed by Northstar Logistics (Pty) Ltd for a period of five years prior to his dismissal, on the basis described to us by our client. On 21 October 2026, our client was instructed to drive a delivery vehicle which he says had faulty brakes. He raised his concern about the safety of the vehicle and asked that the instruction be confirmed in writing. He was not comfortable proceeding with the instruction in circumstances where he held a genuine safety concern.

3. At approximately 08:00 on the same day, our client was advised that a disciplinary hearing would take place at 10:00, some two hours later. The hearing proceeded on that notice. Our client was not permitted to be accompanied by a colleague at the hearing. The hearing was chaired by his direct manager, who had issued the original instruction that gave rise to the allegation. Our client denied that his conduct amounted to insubordination and maintained that his refusal was motivated by a safety concern regarding the vehicle's brakes. He was dismissed immediately following the conclusion of the hearing.

Legal Claims

1. Unfair dismissal: section 188(1) of the LRA and substantive fairness: The fairness of our client's dismissal falls to be assessed under section 188(1) of the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995, which requires both a fair reason for dismissal and a fair process. Applying the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 at paragraphs 7 to 10, the question of substantive fairness turns on whether the conduct alleged occurred, whether it constituted a dismissible offence in the circumstances, and whether dismissal was a proportionate sanction. The allegation against our client was one of insubordination arising from his refusal to drive a vehicle he believed to have faulty brakes. Our client disputes that his conduct amounted to insubordination at all. His refusal was tied to a stated safety concern, and he sought written confirmation of the instruction rather than refusing outright. This context is material to the fairness of treating the refusal as a dismissible offence, and to the proportionality of dismissal as the sanction imposed, particularly in circumstances where our client's service with Northstar Logistics (Pty) Ltd spans a number of years.

2. Procedural fairness: paragraph 11 of the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025: The procedural defects in this matter are, in our view, the dominant feature of this dispute. Paragraph 11 of the Code requires reasonable notice of a disciplinary hearing, a genuine opportunity to prepare, the right to representation by a fellow employee or trade union representative, and an impartial chairperson. Our client was given approximately two hours' notice between the instruction to attend and the hearing itself, which does not reflect a reasonable opportunity to prepare a response or secure representation. Our client was not permitted to bring a colleague into the hearing, denying him the representation contemplated by the Code. Further, the hearing was chaired by the same manager who had issued the instruction underlying the allegation. A chairperson who is also the source of the instruction said to have been disobeyed is not positioned to bring an impartial mind to the proceedings, and this conflation of roles compromises the integrity of the process independently of the substantive merits of the charge.

3. Compensation and remedy: Having regard to the cumulative effect of the matters set out above, our client's position is that the dismissal was both substantively and procedurally unfair within the meaning of section 188(1) of the LRA. The primary remedy under section 193 of the LRA is reinstatement, although our client's present instructions are to pursue a negotiated resolution rather than reinstatement. In the alternative, compensation of up to twelve months' remuneration is available under section 194(1) of the LRA. Given the combination of a disputed substantive basis for dismissal and clear procedural shortcomings in the process followed, our client's exposure assessment of the matter supports a commercially meaningful settlement proposal, calibrated to the litigation risk Northstar Logistics (Pty) Ltd would face before the CCMA.

Without Prejudice Settlement Proposal

Without conceding any aspect of our client's claims, and in the interests of reaching a swift and amicable resolution, our client proposes the following terms of settlement:

• Ex gratia compensation to our client on a total cost to company basis, calibrated to the procedural defects identified above and the available compensation framework under section 194(1) of the LRA, to be agreed between the parties.

• Payment in lieu of the notice period to which our client is entitled under section 37 of the BCEA, subject to any more favourable contractual notice entitlement, such payment to be made under section 38 of the BCEA as payment in lieu of notice not worked

• Payment of accrued but untaken leave pay owed to our client under section 40 of the BCEA.

• Confirmation that any pension or provident fund contributions due in respect of our client are paid up to date, and that the accumulated benefit is dealt with in accordance with the rules of the applicable fund.

• Confirmation that UIF contributions in respect of our client are paid up to date, together with a completed UI-19 certificate.

• A certificate of service in terms of section 42 of the BCEA.

• An agreed reference, in terms to be agreed between the parties, reflecting our client's period of service.

• An undertaking by Northstar Logistics (Pty) Ltd and its representatives not to disparage our client in any communication to prospective employers or third parties.

• Confidentiality as between the parties and their respective advisers regarding the terms of settlement and the underlying negotiations.

• Confirmation that the disciplinary finding against our client is expunged from his personnel record, such that his record reflects no adverse finding arising from this matter.

• The terms above to be recorded in a formal written settlement agreement signed by both parties, with all of our client's rights reserved until such agreement is concluded.

Our client's claims are, in our assessment, well positioned for referral to the CCMA within the applicable 30-day period under section 191(1)(b)(i) of the LRA, and that window remains open at present. Our client would prefer to resolve this matter on a sensible commercial basis rather than proceed to arbitration, and this letter is written in that spirit.

We invite a substantive response to this letter within seven calendar days of receipt, failing which our client reserves the right to proceed to refer this dispute to the CCMA without further notice. All of our client's rights are expressly reserved.

criteria.problem: The expunged-record settlement term and the reference to 'disciplinary finding' assume a disciplinary finding/adverse record entry that is not expressly confirmed in the brief (the hearing resulted in immediate dismissal; there is no mention of a formal finding being recorded separately from the dismissal, or of any other adverse record). This is a minor factual overreach presented as settled fact. Otherwise dates, names, employer, service length and chronology are accurately drawn from the brief.
criteria.required_fix: Reframe to reference expungement of any record of the dismissal or disciplinary process generally, or qualify conditionally ("to the extent any adverse finding or record exists"), rather than asserting a specific disciplinary finding as an established fact.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "Confirmation that the disciplinary finding against our client is expunged from his personnel record, such that his record reflects no adverse finding arising from this matter."

criteria.problem: The draft correctly anchors fairness in section 188(1), applies the 2025 Code, and ties the three confirmed procedural defects (short notice, representation denial, biased chair) and the safety context to substantive and procedural fairness, consistent with the HIGH merit band and the scoring breakdown. It does not overstate certainty and appropriately hedges with 'our client's position is' and 'our client disputes'. Minor weakness: the settlement calibration paragraph is somewhat generic ('commercially meaningful settlement proposal') without explicitly walking through how the specific combination of three procedural defects plus the safety context elevates leverage toward the higher end of realistic outcomes, slightly underusing the strong procedural picture (procedural score 9/10).
criteria.required_fix: Strengthen the exposure paragraph to explicitly connect the near-complete procedural defect picture (notice, representation, bias) to a materially elevated settlement position, without using mandatory 'upper end' language, simply making the causal link more concrete.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "Given the combination of a disputed substantive basis for dismissal and clear procedural shortcomings in the process followed, our client's exposure assessment of the matter supports a commercially meaningful settlement proposal"
